name: Conister Rock
shortDescription: St Mary's Isle (also known as Conister Rock or the Tower of Refuge, Manx: Kione y Sker or Creg Voirrey) is a partially submerged reef in Douglas Bay on the Isle of Man. Prior to 1832 the rock was the property of the Quane family until John Quane, Attorney General of the Isle of Man, presented the rock to Sir William Hillary, in his capacity as President of the Isle of Man District of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution to build the Tower of Refuge.

name: Guernsey
shortDescription: Second-largest Channel Island, with the picturesque harbour of St Peter Port and a strong maritime tradition.
history: Part of the Duchy of Normandy from 933. Occupied 1940–1945 — Castle Cornet's German fortifications still stand.
geography: Higher and more cliff-bound in the south, lower and beachier in the north. The Bailiwick also includes Sark, Herm and Alderney.
transport: Condor Ferries from Poole and Portsmouth; flights into Guernsey Airport from across the UK and Europe.
accommodation: Hotels, guest houses and self-catering across the island, concentrated around St Peter Port.

name: Isle of Man
shortDescription: Self-governing Crown Dependency in the middle of the Irish Sea, famed for the TT motorcycle races and the Manx Gaelic language.
history: Home to Tynwald, often described as the world's oldest continuous parliament (founded c. 979 AD). Norse rule until 1266.
geography: A central upland of slate and shale, with sea cliffs at the Calf of Man and the Sound. The island has its own Manx cat and four-horned Loaghtan sheep.
transport: Steam Packet ferries from Heysham, Liverpool, Belfast and Dublin. Flights into Ronaldsway from many UK and Irish airports.
accommodation: Full range of hotels, guest houses, hostels and self-catering, with a long Victorian seaside tradition in Douglas.

name: Jersey
shortDescription: Largest of the Channel Islands, 14 miles from the French coast — a Crown Dependency with its own parliament and currency.
history: Part of the Duchy of Normandy from 933, retained by the English Crown after 1204. Occupied by Germany 1940–1945.
geography: A south-tilting plateau with extensive sandy bays in the south and rocky cliffs in the north. Famously huge tidal range.
transport: Condor Ferries from Poole and Portsmouth; multiple daily flights into Jersey Airport from across the UK and Europe.
accommodation: Wide range of hotels, guest houses and self-catering across the island; St Helier is the main hub.

name: La Motte
shortDescription: La Motte (French pronunciation: [la mɔt]) is a tidal island, and listed archaeological site, also known as Green Island, located in the Vingtaine de Samarès in the parish of St Clement on the south-east coast of Jersey, Channel Islands. There is evidence of human visits to the island since Neolithic times, having left a cairn, a number of middens and cists which were uncovered in the early 20th century.
